_note: Lane A figure catalogue. Each figure is a FIRST-CLASS OBJECT with its own figure_id, title, caption and labels, so the same figure can be recalled and shown in more than one place: beside a reference entry, beside a question, or on its own. `used_by` lists those places; it is a list, not a single owner. `covers` records which of a linked entry's authored items[] labels this figure renders, and verify.py checks it per entry. `layout` is chosen by the container at render time: compact (272-460px side pane), full (~680px question pane), expanded (enlarge control, notes sheet single column).

chem-pes.title: Photoelectron spectrum
chem-pes.subtitle: Nitrogen (1s2 2s2 2p3): one peak per subshell, height set by electron count
chem-pes.x_label: binding energy (MJ/mol), decreasing to the right
chem-pes.alt: Three peaks on a logarithmic binding-energy axis that decreases to the right, for nitrogen (1s2 2s2 2p3). The 1s peak sits far left at about 39.6 megajoules per mole with height two, then 2s at about 2.45 with height two, then 2p at about 1.45 with height three. Peak height is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell, and the three heights sum to nitrogen's seven electrons. Illustrative values.
chem-pes.note: Electrons closer to the nucleus need more energy to remove.
chem-pes.values_note: Heights (2:2:3) and the binding-energy ordering are exact for nitrogen. The 1s value cross-checks against ~400 eV (~39.5 MJ/mol), but the 2s and 2p figures are standard AP teaching values that I could not trace to a primary table, so the figure is disclosed as illustrative rather than measured.

stats-bar-chart.title: Bar chart of one categorical variable
stats-bar-chart.subtitle: One bar per category; height is that category's frequency
stats-bar-chart.caption: Each bar is one category of a single categorical variable, and its height is the count in that category.
stats-bar-chart.alt: A bar chart with four separated bars, one for each way of travelling to school: car 18, bus 24, walk 12 and bike 6 students, out of 60. The bars stand apart because the variable is categorical, and the vertical axis is a count, so each bar's height is that category's frequency. Illustrative data.
stats-bar-chart.note: Separated bars because the categories have no order. The same heights can show relative frequency instead: 30%, 40%, 20%, 10%.

stats-pie-chart.title: Pie chart of one categorical variable
stats-pie-chart.subtitle: Each slice's share of the area is that category's relative frequency
stats-pie-chart.caption: The same 60 students as the bar chart: each slice's share of the whole circle is that category's relative frequency.
stats-pie-chart.alt: A pie chart of how 60 students travel to school, divided into four slices: bus 40%, car 30%, walk 20% and bike 10%. Each slice's share of the circle's area is that category's relative frequency, and the four slices together make up the whole circle, or 100%. Illustrative data.
stats-pie-chart.note: The four slices sum to 100% of the area, which is what makes a pie chart a display of relative frequency.
covers: Slice area as a fraction of total area
labels: Slice area as a fraction of total area

stats-dotplot.title: Dotplot of a quantitative variable
stats-dotplot.subtitle: One dot per observation, stacked where values repeat
stats-dotplot.caption: Each of the 24 students is one dot, placed above its value, with equal values stacked.
stats-dotplot.alt: A dotplot of the number of pets owned by 24 students. Dots are stacked above each whole-number value on the horizontal axis: three students own none, six own one, five own two, four own three, three own four, two own five and one owns six. Every dot is a single observation and its position is that observation's value. Illustrative data.
stats-dotplot.note: Twenty-four dots for twenty-four students: the height of a stack is how many share that value.

stats-histogram.title: Histogram of a quantitative variable
stats-histogram.subtitle: Ordered bins along the axis; bars meet because the variable is quantitative
stats-histogram.caption: Fifty commute times grouped into six bins of 10 minutes; each bar's height is the count in that bin.
stats-histogram.alt: A histogram of the commute times of 50 adults, in six bins of ten minutes from 0 to 60. The bar heights are 4, 11, 15, 10, 7 and 3 adults, so the distribution peaks in the 20 to 30 minute bin and trails off to the right. The bars touch, because the bins are adjoining intervals of a quantitative variable rather than separate categories. Illustrative data.
stats-histogram.note: Bin width is 10 minutes here; widening or narrowing the bins can change the histogram's apparent shape.

stats-stem-leaf.title: Stem-and-leaf plot
stats-stem-leaf.subtitle: Each value split into a stem and a single-digit leaf, both ordered
stats-stem-leaf.caption: Sixteen test scores: the stem is the tens digit, the leaf the units digit, and the key fixes the scale.
stats-stem-leaf.alt: A stem-and-leaf plot of sixteen test scores. The stems 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 are the tens digits, listed in order down the left of a rule, and each stem's leaves are the units digits in order to its right: 5 gives 2 and 5; 6 gives 1, 3 and 7; 7 gives 0, 2, 4, 8 and 9; 8 gives 1, 5 and 8; 9 gives 1, 3 and 6. The key reads 5 bar 2 means 52, so the plot keeps every original value. Illustrative data.
stats-stem-leaf.note: Unlike a histogram, no information is lost: every individual value can be read back off the plot.

stats-boxplot.title: Boxplot of the five-number summary
stats-boxplot.subtitle: Box from Q1 to Q3, median line inside, whiskers to the extreme non-outliers
stats-boxplot.caption: Twenty-two homework times: the box spans Q1 to Q3, and the two values beyond the 1.5 IQR fence are marked as outliers.
stats-boxplot.alt: A horizontal boxplot of the nightly homework times of 22 students. The box runs from the first quartile at 18 minutes to the third quartile at 30 minutes, with the median line inside it at 22.5 minutes. The left whisker reaches the minimum at 12 minutes and the right whisker stops at 36 minutes, which is the largest value that is not an outlier, rather than at the 48-minute fence. Two outliers at 58 and 62 minutes are marked separately with asterisks. Illustrative data.
stats-boxplot.note: The right whisker stops at 36, the most extreme value that is not an outlier - not at the 48-minute fence.

stats-two-cat-side-by-side.title: Side-by-side bar chart
stats-two-cat-side-by-side.subtitle: Bars for both levels shown within each category (figure 1 of 3)
stats-two-cat-side-by-side.caption: Counts of each level side by side within each year group, so the two levels can be compared directly.
stats-two-cat-side-by-side.alt: A side-by-side bar chart of 150 students by year group and whether they play a school sport. Within each year group a pair of bars shows the two levels: freshmen 24 who play against 16 who do not, sophomores 27 against 33, juniors 30 against 20. Because the bars show counts and the year groups differ in size, the pairs are compared within a group rather than across groups. Illustrative data.
stats-two-cat-side-by-side.note: Counts, not proportions: the year groups have 40, 60 and 50 students, so compare within a pair.

stats-two-cat-segmented.title: Segmented bar chart
stats-two-cat-segmented.subtitle: One bar per category, divided into the levels of the other variable (figure 2 of 3)
stats-two-cat-segmented.caption: One equal-width bar per year group, each divided into the two levels as proportions of that group.
stats-two-cat-segmented.alt: A segmented bar chart of the same 150 students. Each year group is one bar of equal width, divided into the share that plays a school sport and the share that does not: 60% and 40% for freshmen, 45% and 55% for sophomores, 60% and 40% for juniors. Every bar fills the full height, so the display compares proportions within each year group and the differing group sizes are not visible. Illustrative data.
stats-two-cat-segmented.note: Each bar is the same width and full height, so it shows proportions and hides how big each group is.

stats-two-cat-mosaic.title: Mosaic plot
stats-two-cat-mosaic.subtitle: A segmented bar chart whose bar widths show how big each category is (figure 3 of 3)
stats-two-cat-mosaic.caption: As the segmented bars, but each bar's width is its year group's share of all 150 students.
stats-two-cat-mosaic.alt: A mosaic plot of the same 150 students. As in the segmented bar chart each bar is divided into the share playing a school sport and the share not, but here the bar widths differ: the sophomore bar is widest because that year group has 60 of the 150 students, against 50 juniors and 40 freshmen. Each tile's area is therefore the relative frequency of that combination of the two variables. Illustrative data.
stats-two-cat-mosaic.note: Widths are the group sizes, so a tile's area is the relative frequency of that pair of levels.

phys2-pv-isotherm-work.title: PV diagram: the isotherm and the work
phys2-pv-isotherm-work.subtitle: Area under the path is the magnitude of the work (figure 1 of 2)
phys2-pv-isotherm-work.caption: Pressure against volume for a gas expanding along an isotherm; the shaded area is |W|.
phys2-pv-isotherm-work.alt: A pressure-versus-volume diagram for a gas. A single curve falls from upper left to lower right along an isotherm, a line of constant temperature on which the product of pressure and volume is the same at every point. The region between the curve and the volume axis, between the starting and finishing volumes, is shaded: its area is the magnitude of the work for the process. The axes carry no numbers because the diagram teaches the shape, not a measurement. Illustrative data.
phys2-pv-isotherm-work.note: The area gives only the magnitude of W. The gas expands here, so work is done BY the gas and W on the gas is negative.

phys2-pv-special-processes.title: PV diagram: the four special processes
phys2-pv-special-processes.subtitle: Isovolumetric, isobaric, isothermal and adiabatic from one starting state (figure 2 of 2)
phys2-pv-special-processes.caption: Four named processes from the same starting state: vertical, horizontal, along the isotherm, and steeper than it.
phys2-pv-special-processes.alt: A pressure-versus-volume diagram showing four processes leaving the same starting state. The isovolumetric process is a vertical line, because the volume does not change. The isobaric process is a horizontal line, because the pressure does not change. The isothermal process follows the isotherm, on which pressure times volume is constant. The adiabatic process starts at the same point but falls more steeply than the isotherm, because no energy is transferred thermally. Illustrative data.
phys2-pv-special-processes.note: The adiabat is steeper than the isotherm through the same point: that is how the two are told apart.

phys2-potential-around-loop.entry_title: Graph of electric potential versus position in a loop
phys2-potential-around-loop.title: Electric potential around a circuit loop
phys2-potential-around-loop.subtitle: Every rise and drop in one trip round; the net change is zero
phys2-potential-around-loop.caption: Potential against position for a single loop: a 12 V rise across the battery, then 8 V and 4 V dropped across the two resistors.
phys2-potential-around-loop.alt: A graph of electric potential against position as you travel once around a single circuit loop. Starting at zero, the potential rises by 12 volts at the battery, where the tick is marked, stays flat along the connecting wire, drops by 8 volts across the first resistor, stays flat again, then drops by 4 volts across the second resistor, returning to zero. The trace ends at the same potential it started at, because the net change around a closed loop is zero. Illustrative data.
phys2-potential-around-loop.note: The rises and the drops cancel exactly: +12 − 8 − 4 = 0, which is Kirchhoff's loop rule.

used_by.title: Graph of electric potential versus position in a loop

precalc-residual-plot.title: Residual plot
precalc-residual-plot.subtitle: Residuals against the independent variable, with no pattern
precalc-residual-plot.caption: Actual minus predicted, plotted against x: scattered either side of zero with no pattern, which is what justifies the model.
precalc-residual-plot.alt: A residual plot: ten points showing the residual, the actual value minus the value the model predicts, against the independent variable. A horizontal line marks a residual of zero. The points fall on both sides of that line, close to it, with no curve, no fanning and no trend across the plot. That absence of a pattern is what justifies the model as an appropriate fit. Illustrative data.
precalc-residual-plot.note: A curve, or a long run of residuals with the same sign, says the model is the wrong shape; a funnel says the spread is not constant. Either is a pattern.

phys2-mb-qualitative.title: Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution
phys2-mb-qualitative.subtitle: The shape of the curve is set by the temperature of the gas
phys2-mb-qualitative.caption: Atomic energies at two temperatures: the hotter gas is flatter, broader and shifted right.
phys2-mb-qualitative.alt: Two Maxwell-Boltzmann curves showing the relative number of atoms at each energy, for the same gas at two temperatures. The hotter sample's curve has a lower, broader peak shifted to higher energy, while the cooler sample's is taller and narrower. The whole shape of the curve is set by the temperature, which is the feature this diagram exists to teach. Illustrative data.
phys2-mb-qualitative.note: AP Physics 2 asks for the features of the curve, not its functional form.

physcmech-xva-graphs.title: Reading x(t), v(t) and a(t) together
physcmech-xva-graphs.subtitle: Slope of one graph is the value of the next; area under one is the change in the one above
physcmech-xva-graphs.caption: One motion at constant acceleration, shown three ways: slopes read downward, areas read upward.
physcmech-xva-graphs.alt: Three stacked graphs of the same motion against a shared time axis. The top panel is position against time, a curve whose tangent is drawn at one instant: the slope of that tangent is the instantaneous velocity. The middle panel is velocity against time, a straight line whose own slope is the constant acceleration, with the area under it between two times shaded, because that area is the displacement over the interval. The bottom panel is acceleration against time, a horizontal line, whose area over an interval is the change in velocity. Illustrative data.
physcmech-xva-graphs.note: Slopes read downward (x to v to a); areas read upward (a to v to x).

phys-work-force-displacement.title: Work as the area under a force-displacement graph
phys-work-force-displacement.subtitle: Only the component of force along the motion counts
phys-work-force-displacement.caption: The component of the force along the motion, against displacement. The force is constant for the first 2 m, then falls steadily to zero at 6 m; the shaded area is the work it does.
phys-work-force-displacement.alt: A graph of the component of a force along the direction of motion, against displacement. The force holds steady at 8 newtons from 0 to 2 metres, then falls in a straight line to zero at 6 metres. The whole region between that line and the horizontal axis is shaded, because the area under the graph is the work the force does: 16 joules from the flat part and 16 more from the triangle, 32 joules in total. Reading a value off the curve gives a force, not a work; only the area is the work. Illustrative data.

phys2-zero-pressure-temperature.entry_title: Zero-pressure temperature from a P–T graph
phys2-zero-pressure-temperature.title: Finding the zero-pressure temperature by extrapolation
phys2-zero-pressure-temperature.subtitle: The line is extended well past the measurements to reach zero pressure
phys2-zero-pressure-temperature.caption: Pressure of a fixed amount of gas held at constant volume, measured between 0 °C and 100 °C, with the straight line extended backwards until the pressure reaches zero.
phys2-zero-pressure-temperature.alt: A graph of the pressure of a fixed sample of gas at constant volume against its temperature in degrees Celsius. Five measured points from 0 to 100 degrees lie on a rising straight line. That line is continued as a dashed extension far to the left, beyond any measurement, until it crosses zero pressure at about minus 273 degrees Celsius, which is the zero-pressure temperature. The point is reached by extending the line, not by measuring there: no gas stays a gas that cold. Illustrative data.
phys2-zero-pressure-temperature.note: No measurement is taken near −273 °C; the temperature is read off the extended line.

used_by.title: Zero-pressure temperature from a P–T graph
used_by.contract_note: AP Physics 2 9.2 is a convention with no authored items[]; the measured points, the extended line and the zero-pressure temperature it reaches are the contract (DECISION-0116, route b). The entry's body names extrapolation, which is why the extension is drawn dashed and the note says no measurement is taken there.

phys2-ohmic-iv.entry_title: Ohmic materials and the I–ΔV graph
phys2-ohmic-iv.title: Current against potential difference: ohmic and non-ohmic
phys2-ohmic-iv.subtitle: A straight line through the origin is what makes an element ohmic
phys2-ohmic-iv.caption: Current against potential difference for two elements. The ohmic one is a straight line through the origin of slope 0.040 A/V, so its resistance is 25 Ω; the other bends, so no single resistance describes it.
phys2-ohmic-iv.alt: A graph of current against potential difference for two circuit elements, both starting at the origin. The ohmic element gives a straight line: doubling the potential difference doubles the current, so the ratio is fixed and the resistance is constant at 25 ohms. The second element's line curves and flattens as the potential difference rises, climbing away from the straight line, so its ratio of potential difference to current keeps changing and no single resistance describes it. The resistance of the ohmic element is one divided by the slope, not the slope itself. Illustrative data.
phys2-ohmic-iv.note: Resistance is 1/slope here: the slope is 0.040 A/V, so R = 25 Ω.
labels: Ohmic element: a straight line through the origin
Resistance is one over the slope
covers: Ohmic element: a straight line through the origin
Resistance is one over the slope

used_by.title: Ohmic materials and the I–ΔV graph
used_by.contract_note: AP Physics 2 11.3 is a convention with no authored items[]; the straight ohmic line, the bending non-ohmic one and the slope-to-resistance relation are the contract (DECISION-0116, route b). The entry's body says the resistance is found from the slope, so the figure states R = 1/slope rather than leaving the student to assume the slope IS the resistance.
